findings.title: Build large SQLite ID lists without repeatedly copying them
findings.body: When the configured batch size exceeds SQLite’s parameter limit, this loop rebuilds the entire accumulated string for every ID. Constructing a batch of tens of thousands of IDs therefore performs quadratic copying and can allocate gigabytes cumulatively, making cleanup and the large-batch test unnecessarily slow. Use a builder or join preformatted IDs instead.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
findings.body: This log runs after a successful ID query and uses the error level even when `err` is nil; the corresponding cleanup and orphan-tag batch logs do the same. Normal cleanup—including empty final batches—therefore produces error-level events, which can trigger false alerts and flood error logs.

findings.title: The cleanup interval increases tenfold for every cleanup job
findings.body: Changing the ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes the entire cleanup job list run up to ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. This increases recurring database and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and other jobs, despite the PR describing only a change to annotation deletion.

findings.title: Large configured batches can exceed database bind-parameter limits
findings.body: For every non-SQLite database, this creates one bind parameter per selected ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL support at most 65,535 parameters in a statement, so a valid batch-size configuration above that limit will make cleanup fail whenever a batch contains more than 65,535 rows. Split deletes into parameter-safe chunks or otherwise cap the number of bound IDs.
